title: Grandeur in this view
hook: Darwin ends the Origin: there is grandeur in this view of life

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Muir, for whom the mountains were home. Your line was nature's peace will flow into you. Today a naturalist kneels, in words at least, beside a weedy bank.

A bank of earth, overgrown. Weeds tangled together, birds in the bushes, insects in the air, worms working the wet soil. Nobody would put it on a postcard. But it's the picture Charles Darwin chose for the last paragraph of On the Origin of Species: "It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth". From that muddy bank he builds to his final sentence, and its key word is grandeur.
screen: `AN OVERGROWN BANK.` → `NOT A POSTCARD.` → `HIS LAST PARAGRAPH.`

segments.voice: Here is how the book ends: "There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved." First, the entangled bank. Darwin's awe doesn't start with a mountain or a galaxy. It starts with weeds and worms, ordinary life crowded together in the dirt. Second, grandeur, a word for size and splendor, the kind people use for palaces and mountains. Darwin spends it on weeds and worms, and on the long process that made them. Third, two clocks at once. The planet goes "cycling on" by a fixed law, round and round. Meanwhile life branches, from a simple beginning into "endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful." One steady circle, one endless unfolding. Fourth, the tense: "have been, and are being, evolved." Not finished. Still happening, on the bank, in the garden, now. People read this sentence in very different ways. Some people of faith hear in it the wonder of creation still at work. Some with no faith at all find wonder enough in the process itself. Darwin's sentence makes room for both, and both can stand on the same muddy bank and say the same word.
screen: `AN ENTANGLED BANK` · `GRANDEUR FOR WEEDS AND WORMS` · `FROM SO SIMPLE A BEGINNING` · `STILL BEING EVOLVED` · then, large: `GRANDEUR IN THIS VIEW.`

segments.voice: Choose one living thing, a leaf, a houseplant, an insect on the window, a pet, or your own hand, and look at how it's put together: where it branches, where it joins, how one part fits another. Don't name the parts; just follow them with your eyes, slowly, like a path. When your attention drifts, come back to the next joint, the next curve.
Entangled bank. Darwin's image for ordinary life, weeds and worms, from which he saw grandeur: life branching, from so simple a beginning, into endless forms. Today's word.
Your line: endless forms most beautiful. The grandeur starts in the weeds. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path, religious and not, read the last paragraph of the Origin as a meditation on life, and practice slow, close looking at living things in gardens, parks and overgrown corners.

chat.says: Why did Darwin end his big book with a weedy, tangled bank?
options: He found grandeur in ordinary life, still branching into endless forms right there.
He wanted to show nature as a messy struggle with nothing beautiful in it.
It was the spot in his garden where he wrote most of the book by hand.
